en: Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kuśinagara. The Tathāgata was about to enter parinirvāṇa after three months;
he was accompanied by a multitude of bhikṣus and innumerable venerable bodhisattvas who had come to him.
At the place where the Buddha was, they prostrated themselves on the ground, surrounded by their retinues, thirsting for and yearning to hear the Dharma.
The World-Honored One remained silent and did not speak.
The radiance was not bright.
The Venerable Ānanda knelt with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the past and present, when you have preached the Dharma, your radiance has uniquely shone forth."
Now this great assembly is clear and bright, yet it no longer appears.
Why is this so? There must surely be something extraordinary about this.
"I wish to hear its meaning.
The Buddha remained silent and did not respond.
This was repeated three times.
The Buddha told the Venerable Ānanda:
"After my parinirvāṇa,
in an age of the five corruptions when the path of Māra flourishes,..."
Māra has assumed the guise of a bhikṣu to corrupt and disrupt my Way;
he wears secular clothing yet takes pleasure in fine monastic robes of five colors,
drinking wine and eating roasted meat.
They kill living beings out of greed for their taste;
they lack a heart of compassion and harbor mutual hatred and envy.
At that time, there were bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, arhats, and bhikṣus who cultivated virtue through diligent effort;
all honored and respected them as those whom people looked up to.
He taught and transformed others with impartiality;
he took pity on the poor, was mindful of the elderly, and rescued those in distress.
He constantly provided people with scriptures and images for them to revere and serve.
They perform various meritorious deeds;
their disposition is gracious and kind,
and they do not harm others.
One who sacrifices their own body to save other beings does not cherish themselves;
even if such a person exists.
The bhikṣus who were followers of Māra all harbored hatred and jealousy toward him;
they slandered him, spread his ill repute,
and expelled him, driving him away so that he could not remain.
Thereafter, we ourselves failed to cultivate the Way and its virtue;
the temples fell into desolation and ruin, with no one to maintain them,
until they were gradually destroyed.
They merely crave wealth and goods, accumulating them without dispersing them;
they do not perform meritorious deeds,
but instead engage in the buying and selling of slaves and the plowing of fields for cultivation.
He burned forests and mountains,
harming sentient beings without any compassion;
such a person as this is a slave who has become a bhikṣu.
This maidservant has become a bhikṣuṇī;
she possesses no virtue or moral discipline,
being licentious and depraved, making no distinction between men and women.
They cause the Way to become thin and debased;
all this stems from such people as these.
Or perhaps, seeking to evade the local officials, they rely upon my Way to become śramaṇas.
They do not cultivate the precepts;
when the fortnightly assembly for reciting the precepts arrives,
they become weary, indolent, and have no desire to listen.
They abridge and omit the beginning and end, refusing to speak of them in full;
they do not lecture on or read the sutras,
and even those who do read them do not understand the words or phrases.
They speak with forceful words without consulting those who are wise;
they are arrogant and seek fame, exalting themselves to the heavens while regarding dignified deportment as a burden.
These bhikṣus of the Māras hope only for the offerings of others.
After the end of their lives, their spirits shall fall into the Avīci Hell.
Among the five heinous crimes, there is none they shall not pass through. Only after completing as many kalpas of offenses as grains of sand along the banks of the Ganges shall they be released.
He was born in a borderland where the Three Jewels do not exist,
at a time when the Dharma was about to perish;
yet this man and woman were diligent and constantly performed meritorious deeds.
The men were indolent and arrogant, disregarding the words of the Dharma;
they looked upon śramaṇas as if seeing dung and soil,
lacking any faith as the kalpa was about to submerge them.
The deities wept with tears; rains and droughts were不调 (irregular);
the five grains did not ripen; pestilential vapors spread;
and those who died were numerous.
The people toil in hardship;
the local officials oppress them with excessive taxation and do not follow the principles of the Dharma.
Consequently, all long for disorder.
Evil people become as numerous as the sands of the ocean;
because the kalpa is nearing its end, the days and months grow shorter, and those who are virtuous are extremely few—
perhaps only one or two.
Human life is brief and short.
By forty, the hair turns white.
When a man is lustful and his vital essence is exhausted, he meets an untimely end.
The human lifespan is sixty years;
the life span of women is seven, eight, nine, or ten, or even reaches one hundred years.
Suddenly, great floods arise, and the years reach an indefinite limit.
The people of the world do not believe this;
they do not inquire whether one is noble or lowly when they drown and sink,
or are devoured by fish and turtles— whether they be bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, arhats, or bhikṣus.
The various Māras drove him away so that he could no longer participate in the assemblies; instead,
he entered the mountains— a place of merit for those of the Three Vehicles—
and found joy in maintaining a state of serene detachment.
May their lifespans be prolonged and may they be protected by the various devas.
May they encounter the appearance of Candraprabha in the world.
Together, let us promote my Way; [the rest of the text is lost/corrupted]. May they not pass away before the transformation is complete. [The remainder of the inscription is illegible].
